prompt: Each case describes a source of evidence for marketing managers. Name the activity.

cases.text: A bank commissions a four-week study to learn why applicants abandon its online mortgage application.
cases.explanation: A project that collects new data to answer one specific question is marketing research.

cases.text: The e-commerce team analyzes daily checkout data from the firm's own website to forecast next month's orders.
cases.explanation: Ongoing analysis of data the firm already generates, used to predict performance, is marketing analytics.

cases.text: A brand manager receives a weekly digest of competitors' price changes and new packaging regulations.
cases.explanation: Continuous monitoring of competitors and regulation in the external environment is marketing intelligence.

cases.text: An airline conducts a one-time survey of business travellers to decide whether to open a premium lounge.
cases.explanation: New data are collected once, for one decision, so the activity is project-based marketing research.

cases.text: A telecom firm tracks monthly churn from its own customer records to predict which subscribers will leave.
cases.explanation: The data are the firm's own customer records, analyzed continuously: marketing analytics.

cases.text: A food manufacturer continuously follows industry reports on plant-based ingredients and proposed labelling laws.
cases.explanation: Industry developments and regulatory changes are part of the external environment: marketing intelligence.

prompt: Sort each study by the type of research it represents.

cards.text: Quarterly market share tracking reveals a gradual loss in one region.
cards.explanation: Tracking detects a problem that was not yet apparent, so it is problem-identification research.

cards.text: A study estimates the size of an untapped market for electric bicycles in suburban areas.
cards.explanation: A market potential study identifies an opportunity or problem; no choice among actions is being tested yet.

cards.text: An annual brand image survey shows that younger consumers perceive the brand as dated.
cards.explanation: Brand image research brings a hidden problem to light: problem-identification research.

cards.text: Two versions of a television advertisement are tested to select the one to broadcast.
cards.explanation: Advertising testing informs a choice between alternatives, so it is problem-solving research.

cards.text: Three price points for a new subscription plan are compared to choose the launch price.
cards.explanation: Pricing research chooses among alternative courses of action: problem-solving research.

cards.text: Consumers evaluate four concepts for a new snack before one is selected for development.
cards.explanation: A product concept test informs the choice among concepts: problem-solving research.

prompt: Should the firm conduct research? Classify each situation.

options.label: Not justified: findings arrive too late

cases.text: A retailer must choose between two sites for a $20 million flagship store, and its managers disagree about where demand is higher.
cases.explanation: The decision is consequential and the right course of action is uncertain, so research is justified.

cases.text: The chief executive has already signed off a new logo and asks for a survey to show the board that customers like it.
cases.explanation: The decision has been made; the study would serve only to legitimize it.

cases.text: A café owner considers a $15,000 study to decide whether to add a muffin flavour that costs $200 to trial.
cases.explanation: The study would cost far more than the value of the decision it is meant to inform.

cases.text: A competitor launches tomorrow and the firm must set its response price tonight; a pricing study would take six weeks.
cases.explanation: The findings would arrive only after the decision must be made.

cases.text: A car maker is uncertain whether buyers would accept a 10% higher price for a hybrid model to be produced in large volumes.
cases.explanation: A large, uncertain decision: the expected benefit of research is likely to exceed its cost.

cases.text: A manager requests research to confirm a price increase that took effect last month.
cases.explanation: The price has already changed; the research would only legitimize a decision already taken.

prompt: An online grocery service is losing business. Sort each statement: is it a symptom or a possible underlying problem?

cards.text: Online orders fell by 15% this quarter.
cards.explanation: A decline in orders is an observable change, so it is a symptom.

cards.text: Complaints about late deliveries have doubled.
cards.explanation: Increasing complaints are an observable change: a symptom.

cards.text: Fewer customers place a second order.
cards.explanation: Fewer repeat purchases are observed, not explained: a symptom.

cards.text: A new rival service offers free delivery in the same neighbourhoods.
cards.explanation: A new competitor is a possible underlying cause of the decline: a problem.

cards.text: A software update made the checkout page slower to load.
cards.explanation: Slower service is a cause that could produce the symptoms: a problem.

cards.text: A higher delivery fee now exceeds what many students are willing to pay.
cards.explanation: A price increase is a possible underlying cause: a problem.

prompt: Match each management decision problem with its corresponding marketing research problem.

pairs.term: Should the bank close some of its branches?
pairs.match: How often do customers of each branch use in-branch services, and which of them would move to digital channels?
pairs.explanation: The action is closing branches; the information required is branch use and willingness to switch.

pairs.term: Should the airline introduce a fee for seat selection?
pairs.match: What proportion of passengers would pay to choose a seat, and how would the fee affect their choice of airline?
pairs.explanation: The action is a new fee; the information required is willingness to pay and its effect on airline choice.

pairs.term: Should the gym extend its opening hours?
pairs.match: At what times do current and prospective members prefer to train, and how many would visit during the additional hours?
pairs.explanation: The action is longer hours; the information required is preferred training times and expected visits.

pairs.term: Should the cereal brand launch a low-sugar line?
pairs.match: How large is the segment that prefers low-sugar cereal, and what taste and price does that segment expect?
pairs.explanation: The action is a launch; the information required is the segment's size and its expectations.

prompt: A juice brand wants to understand weak sales of its new line. Put the project's activities in the order of the research process.

steps.text: Conduct a problem audit with the brand manager about the weak sales.
State research questions and hypotheses, such as whether shoppers consider the price too high.
steps.explanation: Step 2: developing an approach to the problem.

steps.text: Choose a survey, specify the measures, and define the sample of shoppers.
Field the survey online with 800 shoppers.
Clean the responses and compare ratings across groups of shoppers.
steps.explanation: Step 5: preparing and analyzing the data.

steps.text: Present the findings with a recommendation linked to the pricing decision.
steps.explanation: Step 6: preparing and presenting the report.

prompt: Match each use of AI with the step of the research process in which it occurs.

pairs.match: A model reads the last three board reports and proposes possible reasons why subscription renewals fell.
pairs.explanation: Summarizing background documents and proposing explanations for a symptom belong to problem definition.

pairs.match: A model drafts the screening questions for a study of first-time car buyers.
pairs.explanation: Drafting screening criteria and questions is part of research design.

pairs.match: An AI moderator conducts 300 text-based interviews at the same time, in Spanish and in English.
pairs.explanation: Moderating interviews at scale and in several languages is data collection.

pairs.match: A model assigns 5,000 open-ended complaints to themes such as price, delivery, and staff.
A model drafts a one-page summary for executives and a set of detailed charts for analysts.
pairs.explanation: Drafting summaries and visualizations for different audiences is reporting.

prompt: Each case shows a limitation of AI in marketing research. Name the limitation.

options.label: Simulated consumers are not real consumers
Fluency is not evidence of accuracy

cases.text: A literature summary cites a 2021 journal article on loyalty programmes that does not exist in any library database.
cases.explanation: The reference appears credible but is false.

cases.text: Asked to describe a typical nurse for a persona, a model always describes a woman.
cases.explanation: The model reproduces a bias present in its training data.

cases.text: An analyst asks, "Why do customers love our new design?" and the model lists five reasons why customers love it.
cases.explanation: A leading prompt yields a confirmatory answer.

cases.text: A panel of 500 AI-simulated respondents rates a new snack far more favourably than a later panel of real shoppers.
cases.explanation: The simulated responses appeared plausible but differed systematically from those of real people.

cases.text: Two answers from the same tool, one correct and one incorrect, are written in the same assured and polished style.
cases.explanation: The output has the same apparent confidence whether it is accurate or not.

prompt: Sort each research practice: does it meet the obligations to respondents, or violate them?

cards.text: An online survey states the purpose of the study, how the data will be used, and that participants may stop at any time.
Results are reported as percentages for the whole region, with no names or identifying details.
cards.explanation: Reporting only in aggregate protects respondents' privacy.

cards.text: Transcripts are anonymized and then analyzed with an AI tool that the consent form describes.
cards.explanation: The use of the AI tool falls within the scope of the consent that respondents gave.

cards.text: A caller introduces a "short survey" and ends it by offering a discounted phone plan.
cards.explanation: Soliciting sales under the guise of research is sugging.

cards.text: An analyst pastes interview transcripts, names included, into a public AI chatbot that the consent form never mentioned.
cards.explanation: Uploading the data is a use of it that falls outside the consent respondents gave, and it exposes personal data.

cards.text: A researcher calls a person five times after the person has declined to take part.
cards.explanation: Respondents are not pressured to participate.
